Use this guide to adjust the taxon-centered figures after fitting the [Stratified demonstration](demonstration-stratified.html#taxon-centered). The study contains the full workflow and representative results; this page focuses on plotting controls and selections.

The demonstration defaults to Class and selects Actinomycetes for an individual panel. Reuse `ps`, `strat_path`, `study_tree`, `result_taxa_box`, `result_taxa`, the group contrast and output directory from that study. Choose a taxon from the fitted results when making an individual panel.

```r
available_taxa <- names(result_taxa)[vapply(result_taxa, nrow, integer(1)) > 0L]
stopifnot(length(available_taxa) > 0L)
selected_taxon <- if ("Actinomycetes" %in% available_taxa) "Actinomycetes" else available_taxa[1]
```

## Sankey {#tax2fun-sankey}

Use a Sankey as an overview. Which functional categories connect to each taxon, and where do the selected associations concentrate? Read a wide ribbon as more displayed associations in this view. It is not a direct abundance measurement.

The taxon-centered demonstration selects Class labels in `result_taxa`, omitting Alphaproteobacteria and Candidatus_Peribacteria from this direction. Its boxplots, Chord, dendrogram and signed-effect views reuse the same selection. The function-centered example keeps those classes as possible contributors.

The taxonomy side tree helps you place taxa within their classification. The phylogeny mode instead uses relationships among the matching ASVs. Choose the one that provides the context you want to discuss.

Taxa appear on the left and functional nodes on the right. Ribbon widths count displayed associations. Positive effects use yellow/orange (`#F5BB7C`); nonpositive effects use blue (`#B4CBE0`). Taxonomy and phylogeny are optional side-tree modes.

```r
p_tax_taxonomy <- tax2fun_sankey(
  result_taxa, tree_mode = "taxonomy", physeq = ps,
  tree_options = list(font_size = 16)
)
save_sankey(p_tax_taxonomy, file.path(out, "tax2fun_sankey.html"))


p_tax_phylogeny <- tax2fun_sankey(
  result_taxa, tree_mode = "phylogeny", physeq = ps,
  phylo_tree = study_tree
)
```

Tree tips must match the ASV identifiers in the unagglomerated taxonomy. The tree and taxon endpoint labels share `tree_options$font_size`; long labels retain full hover text.

## Chord {#tax2fun-chord}

What if you want to see how much each selected relationship contributes, rather than how many associations were selected? Use Chord. It connects the fitted results back to the original stratified contributions.

Balanced means give the two group means equal weight, which is useful when group sizes differ. Read ribbon width, effect colour and outer bar height separately. They represent contribution, direction and absolute effect, respectively.

This preview keeps up to ten functions per taxon. Set `max_functions_per_taxon = Inf` to include the complete association set.

Chord width is the mean predicted contribution, with equal weight assigned to the two group means by default. Ribbon colour encodes effect sign; outer bar height encodes absolute effect. Use the same sample subset and rank as the fitted analysis.

```r
p_tax_chord <- tax2fun_chord(
  result_taxa, strat_path, ps, group = group_col,
  contrast = c(reference, target), max_functions_per_taxon = 10,
  draw = FALSE
)
save_chord(p_tax_chord, file.path(out, "tax2fun_chord.html"))

# Pick taxa and functions after inspecting the HTML overview.
chord_taxa <- head(unique(p_tax_chord$links$taxon), 3L)
p_tax_focus <- tax2fun_chord(
  result_taxa, strat_path, ps, group = group_col,
  contrast = c(reference, target), taxa_list = chord_taxa,
  max_functions_per_taxon = 10, draw = FALSE
)
save_chord(p_tax_focus, file.path(out, "tax2fun_chord_focus.html"))
save_chord(p_tax_focus, file.path(out, "tax2fun_chord_focus.pdf"))
head(p_tax_chord$links)
```

Functional labels use `Function name[function ID]`. Narrow sectors may use letter codes; consult the companion label mapping CSV and legend. Category colours encode identity, separately from signed effects. Adjust ribbon and bar opacity using `link_alpha` and `bar_alpha`.

## Contribution boxplots {#tax2fun-box}

After finding an interesting relationship, look at its sample-level distribution. Are most samples shifted, or is the apparent difference concentrated in a few observations? A boxplot helps you inspect variation that is hidden by the summary diagram. Use the same cohort and taxonomic rank as the model so that the two views remain comparable.

The return value is a named list of ggplots. Blue identifies the reference group and yellow/orange the target group for a two-group contrast; these are group colours, not individual effect signs.

```r
result_taxa_box <- result_taxa[selected_taxon]
z <- result_taxa_box[[selected_taxon]]
box_functions <- intersect(c("ko02010", "ko00230", "ko03010", "ko00240", "ko02020"), z$feature)
if (!length(box_functions)) box_functions <- head(z$feature[order(z$p_adjust)], 5L)
result_taxa_box[[selected_taxon]] <- z[match(box_functions, z$feature), , drop = FALSE]
attr(result_taxa_box, "microfun") <- attr(result_taxa, "microfun")
tax_boxes <- tax2fun_box(strat_path, result_taxa_box, ps, group = group_col)
p_tax_box <- tax_boxes[[selected_taxon]]
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "tax2fun_box.pdf"), p_tax_box,
                width = 10, height = 6)
```

## Association dendrogram {#tax2fun-dendro}

A circular dendrogram is useful when you want to organize several taxon–function relationships in one view. Follow a branch from a taxon to its selected functions, and use point size to inspect the absolute modeled effects. The branching is an organization of associations; branch proximity should not be interpreted as evolutionary distance.

Branches organize functions by taxon; point sizes encode absolute model effects. This is an association view, not an evolutionary tree. Use `top_n_per_taxon`; `top_n_per_genus` remains a compatible alias for older code; new examples use `top_n_per_taxon`.

```r
p_tax_dendro <- tax2fun_dendro(
  result_taxa, top_n_per_taxon = 3, label_size = 2.6,
  wrap_width = 20
)$plot
p_tax_dendro <- p_tax_dendro +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.6, 1.6), ylim = c(-1.6, 1.6), clip = "off")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "tax2fun_dendrogram.pdf"), p_tax_dendro,
                width = 10, height = 7.5)
```

The legend follows the result's recorded rank, including Genus or Class. Conflicting explicit ranks are rejected; older result lists without rank metadata need the correct `taxon_level` supplied explicitly.

## Signed model effects {#tax2fun-logfc}

Use signed-effect bars when the main question is direction and magnitude. Start by reading the group contrast, then compare the coefficients. A positive value means a positive target-versus-reference effect under the fitted model; its scientific meaning depends on the model and input scale.

For the MaAsLin2 example, the axis is labelled with its AST coefficient.

```r
tax_effects <- tax2fun_logfc(result_taxa, top_n = 3)
p_tax_effect <- tax_effects[[selected_taxon]] +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "MaAsLin2 AST coefficient")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "tax2fun_effect.pdf"), p_tax_effect,
                width = 8, height = 5)
```

Positive values describe a positive target-versus-reference model effect.  See [export formats](plot-export.html) for the current saving interfaces.
